name: Melanoma
summary: A serious skin cancer arising from pigment-producing cells (melanocytes). Can spread to other parts of the body if not caught early.
keyPoints: Often identified using the 'ABCDE' rule: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter > 6mm, Evolving over time.
Usually irregular or asymmetrical in shape and colour, unlike a harmless mole.
Early detection and removal greatly improve outcomes.

firstAid: Don't attempt to treat, cut, shave, or remove the lesion yourself.
Protect the area from further sun exposure and avoid picking, scratching, or irritating it.
Take a clear photo and note any changes in size, shape, color, or bleeding to show your doctor.
treatment.seekCare: Melanoma needs prompt professional diagnosis and treatment — usually surgical removal, and sometimes additional therapy depending on stage. See a dermatologist or visit a hospital/urgent care as soon as possible. Do not delay or attempt home treatment.

references.label: American Cancer Society — Surgery for melanoma

name: Melanocytic Nevus
summary: Commonly known as a mole — a benign cluster of pigment-producing cells (melanocytes). Almost everyone has at least one.
keyPoints: Can be present at birth (congenital) or appear later in life (acquired).
Usually round or oval, symmetrical, and evenly coloured.
Monitor for changes in size, shape, or colour over time.

firstAid: No treatment is usually needed for a stable, normal-looking mole.
Avoid picking at it, and protect it from sunburn like the rest of your skin.
treatment.seekCare: See a dermatologist if the mole changes in size, shape, or color, starts itching or bleeding, or if you develop a new mole after age 30 — evaluation may include removal for biopsy just to confirm it is benign.

references.label: American Academy of Dermatology — When is a mole a problem?

name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
summary: The most common type of skin cancer, arising in the basal (lower) layer of the epidermis. Grows slowly and rarely spreads to other parts of the body.
keyPoints: Often appears as a skin-coloured plaque or nodule, sometimes with visible blood vessels.
Most common on habitually sun-exposed skin such as the face.
Highly treatable, especially when caught early.

firstAid: Keep the area clean and protected from further sun exposure and trauma.
Avoid picking at any scabbing, crusting, or bleeding on the lesion.
treatment.seekCare: BCC is highly treatable, typically with minor surgery, cryotherapy, or topical therapy, but it needs a dermatologist to diagnose it first. Book an appointment soon — it is rarely an emergency, but should not be ignored.

name: Actinic Keratosis
summary: A rough, scaly patch on the skin caused by cumulative sun (UV) damage. Considered pre-cancerous because it can occasionally progress to squamous cell carcinoma.
keyPoints: Most common on sun-exposed areas: face, ears, scalp, and the backs of the hands.
A patient with more than 10 actinic keratoses has roughly a 10–15% risk of developing SCC.
Several effective treatments exist, including cryotherapy and topical therapy.

firstAid: Apply sunscreen daily and avoid further sun exposure on the patch.
Don't pick, scratch, or try to peel off the scaly area.
treatment.seekCare: See a dermatologist for evaluation — treatments like cryotherapy, topical creams, or photodynamic therapy are simple and effective, and treating it early helps prevent progression to squamous cell carcinoma.

name: Benign Keratosis
summary: A group of harmless, wart-like growths — most commonly seborrhoeic keratosis — recognisable by their sharply demarcated, greasy, 'stuck-on' appearance.
keyPoints: Extremely common: over 90% of adults over 60 have at least one.
Not related to sun exposure in the way actinic keratosis is.
Treatment is usually unnecessary but can be done for cosmetic reasons.

firstAid: No urgent action needed for a typical stuck-on, warty growth.
Avoid scratching or trying to peel it off, which can cause irritation or bleeding.
treatment.seekCare: Usually harmless and treatment is optional. Get any new, changing, itchy, or bleeding spot checked by a dermatologist to confirm it isn't something else, such as melanoma.

name: Dermatofibroma
summary: A common, firm, benign nodule made of fibrous tissue, most often found on the legs. Also known as a fibrous histiocytoma.
keyPoints: Typically 0.5–1.5 cm in diameter, tan to brown in colour.
Characteristic 'dimple sign' — the surface dimples inward when the nodule is squeezed.
Harmless and usually left untreated unless it becomes symptomatic.

firstAid: Avoid squeezing or picking at it.
treatment.seekCare: Dermatofibromas are benign and are usually just left alone. See a dermatologist if it changes shape or color, grows quickly, or becomes painful, so they can confirm the diagnosis.

name: Vascular Lesion
summary: Benign lesions formed by blood vessels, such as cherry angiomas — small, common, red-to-purple papules made of clustered capillaries.
keyPoints: Cherry angiomas increase markedly in number from around age 40 onward.
Appear as firm red, blue, or purple papules, typically 0.1–1 cm.
Not dangerous; removal is only for cosmetic reasons if desired.

firstAid: No first aid is needed for a typical cherry angioma.
If it bleeds after a knock or scratch, apply gentle pressure with a clean cloth until it stops.
treatment.seekCare: These are benign, so treatment (laser, cryotherapy, or electrosurgery) is optional and usually cosmetic. See a dermatologist if a lesion appears suddenly, changes rapidly, or bleeds without an obvious cause.

name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
summary: The second most common type of skin cancer, arising from keratin-producing cells in the epidermis. Usually related to cumulative UV exposure.
keyPoints: Often looks like a scaly or crusty lump that enlarges over time, or a sore that will not heal.
Can occasionally spread (metastasise) if left untreated, unlike basal cell carcinoma.
A prior actinic keratosis, BCC, or melanoma is a strong risk factor.

references.label: DermNet NZ — Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

firstAid: Keep the area clean and covered, and protect it from further sun exposure.
Don't pick at any crusting, or try to treat it with home remedies.
treatment.seekCare: SCC can occasionally spread if left untreated, so see a dermatologist or visit a hospital promptly. Treatment ranges from minor surgery to topical therapy, depending on how early it is caught.

references.label: Skin Cancer Foundation — SCC treatment options

question: What is the ABCDE rule for checking moles?
answer: The ABCDE rule helps spot moles that might be melanoma: Asymmetry (one half looks different from the other), Border irregularity, Color that varies within the same mole, Diameter greater than about 6mm, and Evolving — any change in size, shape, or color over time. A mole with several of these features should be checked by a dermatologist.

question: How can I protect my skin from the sun?
answer: UV exposure is the main cause of most skin cancers and accelerates skin ageing. Effective protection includes using a broad-spectrum sunscreen (reapplied roughly every 2 hours), wearing sun-protective clothing, seeking shade during peak UV hours, and avoiding tanning beds.

question: When should I see a dermatologist about a mole or spot?
answer: See a dermatologist if a mole looks different from your others, is itching, bleeding, or changing in size, shape, or color — or if you develop a new mole after age 30. When in doubt, it's always worth getting it checked.

references.label: American Academy of Dermatology — When is a mole a problem?

question: How often should I do a skin self-exam?
answer: The Skin Cancer Foundation recommends a head-to-toe self-examination of your skin about once a month, plus a full-body exam by a dermatologist at least once a year. If you have a personal or family history of skin cancer, or a lot of moles, self-exams and dermatologist visits should generally be more frequent.

question: What are the risk factors for skin cancer?
answer: Key risk factors include cumulative UV exposure and sunburn history (especially in childhood), fair skin, a family or personal history of skin cancer, having many moles, and immune suppression. UV radiation is the single biggest environmental risk factor for most skin cancers.

question: How are skin lesions diagnosed?
answer: Dermatologists commonly use dermoscopy — examining the skin with a magnifying, illuminated device called a dermatoscope — to look at patterns invisible to the naked eye. This can improve diagnostic accuracy significantly over visual inspection alone, and suspicious lesions are often confirmed with a biopsy.

question: What does DermaScan do?
answer: DermaScan lets you upload or capture a photo of a skin concern and get an AI-assisted estimate of likely conditions, plus a searchable library of ISIC 2019 skin disease categories. It is for education and awareness only — not a medical diagnosis. Always confirm any concern with a licensed dermatologist.
